URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611204873
Iran International, 20 November 2026

“The blockade must be broken,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the ILNA news agency on Friday, when asked about reports that Iranian oil was being loaded for export. Iran would make every effort to export oil and to pursue negotiations, he said.

No Iranian official has confirmed a convoy. But the idea has moved in days from commentary by Revolutionary Guards-affiliated outlets to parliament and, on Friday, to prayer leaders in several cities, a path that decisions taken at the top in Tehran often follow before they are announced. Friday sermons are coordinated nationally by a council that answers to the supreme leader.

The campaign began on Wednesday, when the Guards-affiliated Fars news agency published a commentary urging Tehran to send a convoy of tankers through the blockade.

Iran should announce it officially, Fars said, and warn that any attack on the convoy would bring strikes on the region’s energy infrastructure, “especially UAE oil,” and on communications networks in Dubai.

On Thursday, the oil tracker TankerTrackers said Iran “appears to be preparing to ship out oil again.”

Its co-founder, Samir Madani, told Reuters that a tanker was taking on Iranian crude from another vessel in the Persian Gulf. If it cleared the blockade, it would be the first seaborne export of Iranian crude since mid-July. Al-Monitor reported that more than 14 Iranian tankers were gathered near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil terminal, most with their tracking transponders switched off.

The Guards-affiliated Sabereen News, in a post labeled “unofficial,” said dozens of tankers were preparing to sail for China, and that Tehran had warned governments across the region it would go to war if the United States attacked them.

A Fars report said that any disruption to a tanker’s voyage would mean explosions at oil facilities in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain. Fars illustrated its commentary with an image of Fereydun, the hero of the Persian epic the Shahnameh, on horseback in the sea, guarding Iranian ships.

Mostafa Najafi, described in Iranian media as an adviser to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, linked the plan to the top. The supreme leader had ordered an end to the state of “neither war nor peace,” he wrote, and “the military option is also on the agenda.” Tehran, he wrote, “no longer wants to watch the blockade and the threats.”

Mohammad Bayat, a lawmaker on the presiding board of parliament’s Internal Affairs Committee, called on Friday for tankers to be readied and for “an ultimatum” to Washington and the region’s governments. Iran, he said, “must be the initiator” of practical steps to end the blockade.

In the northwestern city of Ardabil, prayer leader Hassan Ameli, a member of the Assembly of Experts, went furthest.

Officials had taken “a very important decision to break this siege,” he said, and tankers would soon set sail from Kharg for China.

“Our armed forces have warned the Americans that if a single shot is fired at them, all oil centers in the Persian Gulf countries will be Iran’s legitimate target,” he said.

In Tehran, Friday prayer leader Mohammad-Javad Haj-Aliakbari said the armed forces were ready “at sea, on land, in the air, everywhere,” with orders “to take unlimited, unrestricted action, at a time of our own choosing.” “If they want to test us, they can go ahead and test us,” he said.

In Khorramabad, in the west, Friday prayer leader Ahmadreza Shahrokhi urged the armed forces not to let the blockade continue, and said that if any attack came from the territory of the Persian Gulf states, the armed forces should target “the palaces” of their rulers.

In Yasuj, in the southwest, Nasir Hosseini said Iranians wanted the blockade broken “with the power of the nation and the armed forces” and spoke of nuclear deterrence. In Tabriz, Ahmad Motahari-Asl warned that Iran had “not yet closed” the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the mouth of the Red Sea.

The Guards’ commander, Ahmad Vahidi, said: “Today we have put part of a great battle behind us, and part of it lies ahead.”

The blockade has cut Iran off from its main source of foreign currency. Iran loaded about 2 million barrels of crude and condensate a day in March, Reuters reported, citing Kpler and Vortexa. By September, Kpler recorded no loadings at all, the first full month without any since the 1979 revolution. Production has fallen to about 1.8 million barrels a day, roughly half its prewar level.

Chinese refiners usually pay one to two months after delivery, so payments for Iran’s last cargoes could arrive by mid-December, Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler’s head of crude oil analysis, has told Iran International. After that, Tehran stands to lose $3 billion to $6 billion a month.

Alihossein Ghazizadeh, an Iran International analyst, said Tehran had concluded that time was against it. Washington wants to keep the blockade in place until the state is weak enough to collapse, give in or face mass protest, he said, and fighting later would cost the United States less.

“If a war is going to happen in three months, it’s better that it happens today,” he said, describing Tehran’s thinking. Iran could provoke a clash, he said, but the decision to start a full-scale war would rest with the United States and Israel.

The United States has moved the other way. On Wednesday, US Central Command widened the blockade to cover ship-to-ship transfers at sea. “Such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated,” it said, warning that ships failing to comply could face force. CENTCOM says it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June, and in September US forces struck several Iranian tankers near Kharg and Jask after the Guards fired missiles at a US warship.

President Donald Trump has signaled patience. He told Axios this week that he was in no rush to decide on Iran and would see what happened after the new year.

On Thursday he said he could end the war “immediately,” but that Saudi Arabia had asked him “to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who runs the economic campaign, told CNBC this month that death threats against him from Iran’s leadership showed the pressure was working. Of the Guards, he said: “They’re like a dangerous cornered animal.”

Israel has pressed the other way. Mossad chief Roman Gofman was in Washington last week to urge a resumption of joint strikes, Axios and the Wall Street Journal reported.

If the tankers sail, Washington faces a choice it has so far avoided: let the blockade break, or fire on Iranian ships and test whether Tehran will carry out its threat against the Persian Gulf states.

"])•••$RC("B:5","S:5")More StoriesIraq begins taking back town held for a decade by Iran’s strongest militia allyNov 20, 2026, 10:24 GMT+0Listen to this article100%Members of the Iraqi police take part in a security deployment on the outskirts of Jurf al-Sakhar, Babil province, Iraq, November 20, 2026.Iraqi forces began deploying on Friday in Jurf al-Sakhar, a town south of Baghdad held for more than a decade by Iran’s most powerful militia ally in Iraq, under a deal brokered by Shiite leaders days after the head of Iran’s Quds Force arrived in Baghdad.

A convoy flying Iraqi flags drove toward Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, and hundreds of soldiers took up positions on the outskirts.

The yellow flags of Kataib Hezbollah were still flying farther inside the town, and none of the group’s fighters were visible. A security headquarters is due to open on Saturday to oversee the handover, with a unit assigned to protect energy facilities.

Under the deal, Kataib Hezbollah fighters are to withdraw to other parts of Iraq, Reuters reported, citing security officials. Al Arabiya, citing sources, said the withdrawal would be phased over a month. A joint command of the army, federal police, energy police and units of the Popular Mobilization Forces is taking over the town.

The standoff began on Monday, when Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered troops to prepare to enter Jurf al-Sakhar after an investigation accused Kataib Hezbollah of running a network that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state oil through tampered pipelines.

Nine senior security and oil officials were dismissed, and arrests linked to the case raised fears of an armed confrontation. The group denies the accusations and had warned it would resist any attempt to enter the town.

The same day, Esmail Qaani, commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, which runs Iran’s network of allied armed groups abroad, arrived in Baghdad to help defuse the crisis, Iraqi Shiite political sources told Reuters. Kataib Hezbollah said its leader, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani and Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Iran-backed Badr Organization, in the talks that led to the deal.

Jurf al-Sakhar, a Sunni farming town on the Euphrates about 50 kilometers south of Baghdad, was retaken from Islamic State in 2014 by the army and Shiite militias, Kataib Hezbollah among them. Its residents were never allowed back. More than 100,000 people from the town and surrounding villages remain displaced, Shafaq News reported, and even government officials have rarely been let in.

The town sits near the roads linking Baghdad with Karbala and Anbar province, and has served as a financial hub for evading sanctions on Iran, said Omar Mohammed, an Iraqi historian known for documenting life under Islamic State as Mosul Eye. He called the move “a theatrical show.”

“I think maybe the Iranian-backed militias will allow them some cosmetic gains, but there’s no way that Iran is going to allow its footprint in Iraq to disappear,” David Patrikarakos, a journalist and author of a book on Iran’s nuclear program, told Iran International earlier this week.

Kataib Hezbollah was founded after the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq by Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, who was killed alongside Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani in a US drone strike at Baghdad airport in January 2020. Washington designated it a terrorist organization in 2009 and blamed it for a January 2024 drone attack that killed three US soldiers at a base in Jordan.

It is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella of Iran-backed factions that has claimed more than 150 attacks on US forces since the Gaza war began in 2023, and more recently on US troops in the Persian Gulf states.

The militias report directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. Their arsenals include anti-tank guided missiles, precision-guided rockets, armed drones and some short-range ballistic and cruise missiles, according to Iraqi security officials.

Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of fighters and no announced leadership structure. It forms several battalions of the Popular Mobilization Forces, an umbrella of mostly Shiite armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and later made an official state force.

Its fighters draw state salaries, and some of its members designated as terrorists by the United States hold senior posts in the PMF. It also has a political party, Huquq, with five lawmakers, and business interests in construction, housing, trade and currency exchange, according to an Iraqi official report. The group denies these.

Since the United States and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, Iraqi militias have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. President Donald Trump has pressed Zaidi to disarm them, and the factions have refused to hand over their weapons.

100%Members of the Iraqi police take part in a security deployment on the outskirts of Jurf al-Sakhar, Babil province, Iraq, November 20, 2026.A risky test for BaghdadMoving against the militias carries a price. In November 2021, after then-Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi ordered a crackdown, his Baghdad home was hit by an armed drone in what officials called an assassination attempt.

In August, Iraqi special forces arrested the intelligence chief of another Iran-aligned faction, Harakat al-Nujaba, over drone attacks on US targets. He was released 48 hours later after threats of retaliation and the intervention of senior Shiite politicians.
